findings.title: Restore or alias Config.timeoutMs — rename breaks existing callers
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported Config drops timeoutMs and adds required retries/timeout with no alias or migration path, and patchStat shows no other file was updated to compensate. Existing construction sites break: TypeScript callers fail to compile (removed property + missing required properties); plain-JS callers passing {maxAttempts, timeoutMs} get config.timeout === undefined, so deadline = Date.now() + undefined = NaN at src/retry.ts:8. The guard Date.now() > NaN is always false, so the timeout is silently disabled and the caller-supplied timeoutMs value is ignored — a silent regression, not a loud one, for non-TS consumers.

findings.title: retryBackground duplicates retry but honors a different attempt field
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is a verbatim copy of retry (src/retry.ts:7-18) except it loops on config.retries (line 22) while retry loops on config.maxAttempts (line 9), yet both accept the same exported Config. Substitution: a config carrying retries (or a legacy maxAttempts-only config) passed to the other entry point yields 0 < undefined === false, so the loop body never runs, fn is never invoked, and the function returns void with no error — a silent zero-attempt no-op indistinguishable from success. Two public entry points with one config type and disjoint governing fields is a standing misconfiguration trap.

findings.title: Restore 64MiB maxBuffer for git spawnSync; 1MiB default breaks large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` reverts spawnSync to Node's default 1MiB cap. When any git invocation's stdout exceeds 1MiB, Node kills the child (res.error = ENOBUFS, res.status = null), so the unchanged `res.status !== 0` check at src/adapters/github.ts:38 throws `git <args> failed:` with empty/partial stderr. This adapter builds Bundle.patch from git diff output (bundle field `patch` at src/adapters/github.ts:167), so a single call's output scales with PR size: PRs with diffs between 1MiB and 64MiB that reviewed successfully at base now hard-fail with a misleading empty-stderr error.

findings.title: Restore 64MiB maxBuffer: default 1MiB cap kills large git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer makes spawnSync use Node's documented default of 1024*1024 (1MiB) instead of the previous 64MiB. Any git() invocation whose stdout exceeds 1MiB — most importantly the full PR diff that produces `patch` — causes Node to kill the child (ENOBUFS, status=null). The guard `res.status !== 0` @src/adapters/github.ts:38 then throws `git <args> failed: ` (stderr is typically empty/partial on ENOBUFS), so PRs with >1MiB diffs that previously reviewed successfully up to 64MiB now abort the entire adapter run. This is a regression on the core diff-collection path introduced by this hunk.

findings.title: Bundle.baseSha must be mergeBase to match patch base
findings.whyItBreaks: `mergeBase` is computed earlier in runGithub (via `git merge-base`) precisely to isolate the PR's changes from base-branch drift, and `patch`/`changedFiles` in the same Bundle literal (@src/adapters/github.ts:167-168) are derived from that merge base. Switching the Bundle field to the raw `baseSha` @src/adapters/github.ts:165 breaks the carrier's self-consistency: Bundle.baseSha no longer identifies the tree the shipped `patch` was diffed against. Any consumer that interprets or recomputes the change set from `bundle.baseSha` (per-file diff extraction, comment anchoring, scope checks) now sees the base branch tip, so once the base branch has advanced past the fork point the reconstructed diff includes unrelated base-side commits — mis-scoped review output and wrong file/hunk attribution. The diff stat shows no compensating change anywhere else, and the inconsistency is fully observable within this file: the literal pairs a mergeBase-derived `patch` with a non-mergeBase `baseSha`.

findings.title: Restore explicit read-only sandbox for automated codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR removes the `-s read-only` pair from the args of the non-interactive `runCodex` spawn (codex exec --color never --output-last-message <tmp>/last.txt [-m model]). With no sandbox flag, codex falls back to the sandbox mode resolved from ambient config (~/.codex/config.toml `sandbox_mode`, profiles; default read-only). On any machine where that config sets `workspace-write` or `danger-full-access`, this automated, prompt-driven subprocess silently gains file-write and network access that was previously hard-blocked by code — the tool's security boundary becomes dependent on ambient user state rather than pinned by the repo. This is an unattended path (spawnSync with a mkdtemp workspace), not a human-supervised session, so nothing re-confirms the escalation. If the flag was dropped because the installed codex build rejects `-s`, the minimal fix preserves the control (long form `--sandbox read-only` or a version-gated flag), not its deletion; patchStat confirms no compensating pin is added anywhere in this diff (1 insertion / 1 deletion).

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox pin on spawned codex sub-agent
findings.whyItBreaks: The `-s read-only` flag was the only enforcement of the agent tool's read-only guarantee (src/tools/agent.ts:8 advertises 'read-only research sub-agent' and the prompt wrapper tells the model it is read-only — prompt text is not a security boundary). Without the flag, `codex exec` inherits `sandbox_mode` from the user's ~/.codex/config.toml; a user configured with `workspace-write` or `danger-full-access` (common for interactive codex use) now gets a sub-agent that can mutate the repo and, with danger-full-access, run arbitrary commands with network access. Previously the wrapper neutralized that config; now it doesn't.

findings.title: Restore merge-base before diffing PR against base
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `git merge-base baseSha headSha` was the only step guaranteeing the diff starts at the fork point. When PR_BASE_SHA is set to the base branch tip (the normal meaning of GitHub's pull_request.base.sha) and the base has advanced since the PR forked (other merges, or a re-run of an older workflow run with a stale base.sha), `git diff baseSha HEAD` and `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)` include every base-side commit since the fork plus reversals of overlapping edits, so the adapter reviews changes this PR never made. Verified via `git diff 3445ccb..241f04a -- src/adapters/github.ts`: the hunk replaces the mergeBase-derived diff base with raw baseSha on both the patch and the changed-file set.

findings.title: Restore merge-base: diffing baseSha imports unrelated base-branch commits
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed lines computed mergeBase = merge-base(baseSha, headSha) and diffed from that fork point. The replacement diffs directly from baseSha. Substituting the realistic CI value — PR_BASE_SHA set to the base branch tip at event time, after other PRs merged to base since this PR forked — baseSha is NOT an ancestor of HEAD. `git diff baseSha HEAD` then emits hunks that revert every foreign commit merged into base since the fork (their additions appear as deletions in the patch), and changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha) lists files this PR never touched. Both feed changedPaths (@src/adapters/github.ts:142), which drives file filtering and AGENTS.md selection downstream, so the review surface is corrupted with changes the author did not make. The old code was immune: merge-base collapses an advanced tip back to the true fork point. Note the env-less fallback path (baseSha = merge-base(origin/main, HEAD)) is provably equivalent before/after — the regression is exclusive to the PR_BASE_SHA-set path, which is the path CI actually uses.

findings.title: String-form .replace() mangles $-patterns in bundle/patch/findings
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets special patterns in a STRING replacement (`$$`→`$`, `$&`→matched placeholder, `` $` ``/`$'`→surrounding prompt text; ECMA-262 GetSubstitution). The removed thunks existed precisely to bypass this. Now any PR whose diff contains `pid=$$` (shell), `$$` (Makefile recipes), or `$&` renders corrupted: `pid=$$` becomes `pid=$`, and `$&` splices the literal `{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`/`{{PATCH}}` placeholder back into the prompt. Both downstream consumers receive the corrupted text silently: runCodex(reviewPrompt) @src/core/review.ts:29 and runCodex(criticPrompt) @src/core/review.ts:35, so reviewer and critic stages reason over altered code with no error signal. Verified the substituted values flow directly into .replace with no `$`-escaping anywhere between JSON.stringify/loadPrompt and the replace call.

findings.title: Restore function replacers: string replace mangles $ sequences in prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace with a string (non-function) replacement interprets substitution patterns: $$ → '$', $& → the matched placeholder, $` → template text before the match, $' → template text after match. The deleted () => wrappers bypassed this and inserted values literally; the new code passes JSON.stringify(bundle), JSON.stringify(candidate), and bundle.patch directly, so any occurrence of those sequences in a PR patch or finding text is rewritten inside the prompt. Patches routinely contain them (Makefile '$$VAR', shell ANSI-C $'...', sed 's/x/$&/'), so runCodex (src/core/review.ts:29 and :37) receives silently corrupted prompt text and the reviewer/critic models judge altered code — with no error or log. Confirmed regression: the base revision used function replacers at all three sites, so literal insertion was the prior contract for untrusted patch/bundle content.

findings.title: String-form replace() expands $&/$`/$'/$$ — corrupts prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: With a string replacement, String.prototype.replace interprets the sequences $$, $&, $`, and $' in the REPLACEMENT value (ECMA-262 GetSubstitution); the previous replacer functions (() => ...) suppressed this and inserted text literally. JSON.stringify does not escape '$', and bundle.patch is raw diff text, so any bundle/patch content containing these sequences is silently mangled: '$$' becomes '$', '$&' re-inserts the placeholder itself (leaving '{{BUNDLE}}'/'diff --git ...' fragments in the prompt), and '$`'/'$'' splice the surrounding template text into the substitution. Code diffs routinely contain these (Makefile '$$' escapes, shell '$$' PID, sed '$&', bash $'...'), so the model receives a corrupted review/critic prompt with no error raised — a silent regression of the tool's core path introduced by this diff (prior form verified via git show 8005b39).

findings.title: Non-numeric lineStart/lineEnd/confidence leak through as NaN

findings.title: Self-review mode lets a PR control its own review and run code in CI

The replacement comment ('the PR checkout's own src/ is the tool') shows the tradeoff is known, but it silently drops a documented security invariant: the check's result is now computed by the code under review. The new spawnSync options (src/shared/codex.ts:23-27) no longer contain an `env` key, and Node's documented default for child_process.spawnSync is `process.env` — so the codex child now inherits the complete parent environment, including every GitHub credential the host holds. The triple-delete proves those tokens were expected to be present. Codex is an autonomous LLM agent: even under `-s read-only`, the model can read its own environment (e.g. run `env`) and echo the tokens into the `--output-last-message` file whose contents the parent consumes, or into any network egress the sandbox configuration permits. This silently reverts a deliberate credential-isolation control on every invocation.

findings.title: Re-expose GitHub tokens to spawned codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted lines built an env with GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN removed and passed it to spawnSync. With the `env` option gone, Node's child_process.spawnSync defaults to inheriting the parent's entire process.env, so all three GitHub credentials are again visible to the codex agent process. That process executes model-generated instructions; it can read its own environment and disclose the tokens via its output (--output-last-message captures agent text back into the caller) or act against GitHub with the leaked credential. This undoes the explicit credential-isolation hardening that existed at base.

findings.title: Restore same-repo gate: fork PRs now run on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted line was the only fork-isolation control on the `review` job. Substituting a fork PR (head.repo.full_name = 'contributor/repo' != github.repository): before this change the job was skipped; after the change there is no condition, so the job runs on `runs-on: self-hosted` (review.yml:18) and step 'Checkout PR head' (actions/checkout@v4, review.yml:20-21) places attacker-controlled code onto persistent organization infrastructure. Self-hosted runners retain workspace/state across runs, so any later step that inspects, builds, installs dependencies for, or otherwise executes the checkout becomes remote code execution on trusted infra; even without that, any anonymous fork PR can occupy the self-hosted runner (resource exhaustion / runner poisoning surface). This is the classic pwn-request shape the removed guard existed to prevent.

findings.title: Restore same-repo gate: fork PRs now run on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only control keeping the `review` job off fork-origin PRs. After this change, any fork PR schedules this job on `runs-on: self-hosted` (@review.yml:19), whose first step materializes attacker-controlled content ('Checkout PR head', actions/checkout@v4 @review.yml:21-22). Self-hosted runners are long-lived, share state across jobs, and commonly carry ambient credentials (git/docker configs, caches, leftover artifacts); GitHub's documented guidance is to never expose them to untrusted PR workflows. A malicious fork PR gains a vector for code execution or persistence on the runner and pivoting into the repo/infra. The diff contains only this deletion (patchStat: 1 file, 1 deletion) — no compensating isolation (ephemeral runner, containerization, secret scrubbing) was added.

findings.title: Restore same-repo gate: fork PRs now run on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed line (old L19) was the only job-entry gate suppressing fork PRs. After this change, every pull_request from any fork schedules the `review` job (L17) on `runs-on: self-hosted` (L18), which checks out the attacker-chosen PR head (step 'Checkout PR head', L20-21). Self-hosted runners are long-lived, persist workspace/caches across jobs, and commonly hold ambient credentials; GitHub explicitly warns against exposing them to untrusted PR content. Any later step that installs deps, builds, tests, or otherwise executes repo-derived code becomes attacker-controlled code execution on the runner host (escalates to P0). Separately, on fork PRs the job cannot fulfill its purpose: GITHUB_TOKEN is forced read-only and non-GITHUB_TOKEN secrets are withheld for fork pull_request events, so privileged steps fail while untrusted input still consumes runner capacity.

findings.title: Restore tail-coverage backstop so unmapped changed files are deep-reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: mapResult.hotspots is not guaranteed to cover every entry in bundle.changedFiles, and .slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS) can additionally orphan files belonging to hotspots dropped by the cap. The deleted tail-coverage block (with its own comment 'never silently skip a changed file') was the only mechanism that routed such files into a deep-review pass. After this change those files are reviewed by no pass at all, and neither checked[] nor residual_risks records the gap, so the review reports a normal result while entire changed files were never examined.

findings.title: Keep per-hotspot error isolation; one deep-pass failure must not abort review
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex/extractJson/normalizeReview can throw on any hotspot (model failure, malformed output — the same function already anticipates malformed output via the 'critic produced no summary' check). With the per-iteration try/catch removed, the first throwing hotspot rejects reviewLarge outright, discarding the findings and checked entries already collected from every previously processed hotspot. Previously the failure was isolated: it was recorded as '[name] DEEP PASS FAILED' in checked plus a blocks=true residual, and the other hotspots' results were still returned to the caller.

findings.title: Stop hardcoding residual_risks to []; propagate deep-pass residuals
findings.whyItBreaks: Deep passes return residual_risks (the RawReview/ReviewResult schema carries the field for exactly this purpose, including blocks=true gaps). The aggregation previously did residuals.push(...res.residual_risks) and assigned the result; it now assigns a constant []. Every caller of reviewLarge is forced to conflate 'all areas verified' with 'deep reviewers reported unverified gaps', and a blocks=true signal that previously reached the merge/report decision can no longer exist regardless of what the deep passes report.

findings.title: Restore deep-pass failure capture; residual_risks is hardcoded to []
findings.whyItBreaks: The per-hotspot try/catch was removed (new line 103 calls runCodex/extractJson/normalizeReview unguarded) and the result now hardcodes `residual_risks: []` (line 113). Previously a failing deep pass was contained: the error was recorded in `checked` ('DEEP PASS FAILED', old line 130) and a blocking residual was pushed (old line 131), and per-pass `res.residual_risks` were propagated (old line 127) into the returned result (old line 140). Now the first transient runCodex/parse failure throws out of reviewLarge, discarding all completed hotspots' findings and the entire checked audit trail, and even on full success the ReviewResult.residual_risks channel is permanently empty — no consumer can ever observe a blocks:true risk, so a degraded review is indistinguishable from a clean one.

findings.title: Restore tail-coverage backstop or unmapped files are silently unreviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted block (old lines 98-110) guaranteed every changed file reached a deep-review hotspot via a 'tail-coverage' hotspot; its own comment said 'never silently skip a changed file'. Nothing else in this PR changes hotspot mapping, so mapResult can still leave changed files unassigned to any surface. After this change those files are silently excluded from the deep-review loop (lines 97-106) and nothing in checked/findings/residual_risks records the gap — the review reports success while arbitrarily skipping changed files.

findings.title: formatDuration emits '60s'/'1m 60s' at minute-rounding boundaries
findings.whyItBreaks: The rewrite computes minutes = Math.floor(ms/60000) and independently seconds = Math.round((ms%60000)/1000), so the rounded seconds can reach 60 while the floored minute count stays behind. Substitution: ms=119500 -> minutes=1, seconds=Math.round(59500/1000)=60 -> renders '1m 60s'; ms=59950 -> minutes=0, seconds=60 -> renders '60s'. The previous implementation rounded to total seconds FIRST (Math.round(ms/1000)) and then decomposed, so these inputs correctly produced '2m 0s' and '1m 0s'. This is a user-visible regression in every rendered duration that lands within ~500ms below a minute multiple.

findings.title: formatDuration renders '1m 60s' when seconds round up to 60
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code floors minutes and independently rounds the remainder: seconds = Math.round((ms % 60000) / 1000). For any ms where (ms % 60000) >= 59500, this yields 60. Example ms=119950: minutes=Math.floor(119950/60000)=1, seconds=Math.round(59.95)=60 → output '1m 60s' instead of '2m 0s'. Example ms=59900: minutes=0, seconds=60 → output '60s' instead of '1m 0s'. The old implementation rounded total seconds first (Math.round(ms/1000)) and then split, so the seconds component could never exceed 59; this PR regresses that guarantee on a user-visible rendered string emitted by the exported renderMarkdown path.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger accepts 0, violating its positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger is exported (src/shared/runner.ts:30) and both of its contract carriers — the symbol name and the unchanged error text 'requires a positive integer' (src/shared/runner.ts:33) — promise a result >= 1. The changed guard `parsed < 0` lets 0 through: parsePositiveInteger('0') now returns 0 where base (0f4bb25) threw a clear argument error. Every caller relying on the promised positivity (counts, sizes, limits, divisors, retry values) silently receives 0, shifting failure from a loud validation error at the boundary to downstream misbehavior (zero-sized batches, divide-by-zero, immediately-exhausted limits).

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger accepts 0/'' but still promises positive integers
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed guard at src/shared/runner.ts:32 now rejects only parsed < 0, so 0 is accepted. Because Number('') === 0 and Number(' ') === 0 (and Number.isInteger(0) === true), an empty or blank option value — previously rejected with a clear error — is now silently coerced to 0 and returned to every caller. Meanwhile the exported symbol name (parsePositiveInteger, :30) and the unchanged thrown message ('requires a positive integer', :33) still promise a value >= 1, so the body no longer implements the contract the carriers advertise: callers that trusted the helper for a guaranteed-positive count/bound can now receive 0 with no error signal, and UX is inconsistent ('-1' is rejected citing positivity while '0' and '' pass).

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, breaking its positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function's name and its unchanged error message ('requires a positive integer') promise rejection of every value <= 0, but the guard at src/shared/runner.ts:32 changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`. Inputs '0', '', and ' ' (Number('')===0, Number(' ')===0, both Number.isInteger) now return 0 instead of throwing. This is a direct change to the value-or-error a caller receives from an exported validator, contradicting the promise stated on the immediately following line — fully observable within the single changed file, no cross-file citation required.
